reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: A juvenile-onset axial spondyloarthritis sharing strong HLA-B27 association and clinical features with enthesitis-related arthritis
In children, peripheral arthritis and enthesitis of the lower limbs and hips often precede axial symptoms by years
Inflammatory back pain (worse at rest and in the early morning, improving with activity) and buttock pain from sacroiliitis mark axial disease
Hip involvement is common in juvenile-onset disease and is an important cause of long-term disability
Acute symptomatic anterior uveitis (painful red eye) can occur, in contrast to the chronic silent uveitis of oligoarticular JIA
MRI detects active sacroiliitis before plain radiographs show structural change, aiding early diagnosis
Management uses NSAIDs and physiotherapy first line, with TNF inhibition for persistent axial disease or inadequate response
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis is an axial spondyloarthritis in which HLA-B27-associated immune dysregulation, with prominent involvement of the interleukin-23/interleukin-17 pathway, drives inflammation at entheses, sacroiliac joints and the spine. Enthesitis and osteitis are followed by reparative new bone formation, which over time can produce syndesmophytes, joint fusion and progressive loss of spinal and sacroiliac mobility. Because the skeleton is still growing, hip and axial involvement in childhood can have particularly significant functional and structural consequences.
additionalDifferentials: Enthesitis-related arthritis and other juvenile spondyloarthritis
Mechanical back pain and postural causes
Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis affecting the spine
Malignancy involving the spine or pelvis
additionalInvestigations: HLA-B27 typing to support the diagnosis
MRI of the sacroiliac joints and spine to detect early inflammatory change
Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein)
Radiographs of the sacroiliac joints and spine in established disease
Assessment of spinal mobility and posture for monitoring
Ophthalmology review for symptomatic anterior uveitis
Screening for inflammatory bowel disease when gastrointestinal symptoms occur
redFlags: Progressive loss of spinal mobility or fixed deformity
Acute painful red eye requiring urgent ophthalmology assessment
Neurological symptoms or severe night pain suggesting an alternative serious cause
Systemic features suggesting infection or inflammatory bowel disease
reference.prognosis: Juvenile-onset disease tends to have more peripheral and hip involvement than adult-onset ankylosing spondylitis and can progress to significant axial disease and disability over years. Early diagnosis, physiotherapy and TNF inhibition improve symptom control and may limit structural progression.
pitfalls: Attributing inflammatory back and buttock pain to mechanical causes and delaying imaging
Relying on plain radiographs, which are insensitive to early sacroiliitis
Underestimating hip disease as a driver of disability
Assuming HLA-B27 negativity excludes the diagnosis
Missing associated uveitis or inflammatory bowel disease
references: ASAS criteria for axial spondyloarthritis (adapted to juvenile disease)
